name: Battle of the Kalka River
info: On 31 May 1223 a Mongol force under Jebe and Subutai defeated Cumans and Rus' princes at the Kalka River, in present-day Donetsk Oblast, and then killed the Kievan prince and his nobles after their camp surrendered.

facts.date: 31 May 1223; by another reckoning the main defeat came three days earlier and the fighting ended, at the Kievan camp, on 31 May
facts.place: The Kalka River, now in Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine; the river's location is not known for certain, and it is thought to be the Kalchyk, which flows into the Sea of Azov
facts.sides: Rus' princes, among them Mstislav the Bold of Galicia, Mstislav III of Kiev and Mstislav of Chernigov, with no commander-in-chief, and the Cumans under Köten, against the Mongols under Jebe and Subutai. Strengths are estimates: for the Rus' from 8,000 (Sverdrup) to 80,000 (Gabriel, Munro); for the Mongols 20,000 (de Hartog) or about 23,000 (Gabriel).
facts.outcome: The Mongols won. The Cumans and most of the Rus' hosts were routed, the Kievan camp surrendered after three days, and its princes were killed. The Mongols did not go on to Kiev and turned east.

t: No primary source gives the numbers. Estimates of the Rus' army run from 8,000 to 80,000 and more, and John Fennell calls many of the figures in the Russian sources formulaic or exaggerated.

The Rus' princes had no joint commander. Each retinue acted on its own prince's decision, and the host of Kiev stayed behind a camp on the west bank while the others crossed the river and were beaten.
The Mongols did not stay. They pursued the survivors to the Dnieper, turned east, and came back in 1237 under Subutai and Batu Khan.
dyk: On their expedition Jebe and Subutai rode 5,500 miles (8,900 km) in three years, and Subutai left spies in Rus' who reported on what was happening there and in Europe.
ev: Genghis Khan invades the Khwarezmian Empire, which breaks up over the next three years
A Georgian army is destroyed by Jebe and Subutai at Khunan and King George IV Lasha is mortally wounded
The Mongols persuade the Cumans to leave their alliance with the Alans and then invade the Cuman steppe
Köten's appeal brings the Rus' princes together, and they have the Mongol envoys killed and move down the Dnieper
On 31 May the allies cross the Kalka River and the Cumans and most of the Rus' hosts are routed
The Kievan camp surrenders after three days and its princes are killed
The Mongols turn east and are beaten by the Volga Bulgars at Samara Bend
Subutai and Batu attack again and conquer the Kievan Rus'

sections.background:
In 1219 Genghis Khan invaded the Khwarezmian Empire in retaliation for the murder of his ambassadors, and over three years his armies destroyed its forces and the empire broke up. When Jebe, one of the generals pursuing the Sultan Ala ad-Din Muhammad, heard that the Sultan had died, he asked Genghis Khan for a year or two to continue his conquests before returning to Mongolia by way of the Caucasus. While awaiting the answer, Jebe and Subutai, each commanding a tumen, led an army of 20,000 men through Persian Iraq and Azerbaijan, sacking Rey, Zanjan and Qazvin. In late 1221 they entered Georgia again and destroyed a Georgian army at Khunan.

Genghis Khan then gave his permission. The crossing of the Caucasus cost the Mongols their siege engines and hundreds of men lost to the cold. North of the mountains they met an alliance of Lezgians, Alans and Cherkesses, joined by the Cumans, whom the Mongols persuaded to leave it by reminding them of Turkic-Mongol friendship and promising a share of the booty. They routed the rest and then turned on the Cumans, who fled north-west. The Cuman khan Köten went to his son-in-law Mstislav the Bold of Galicia and warned him: "Today the Mongols have taken our land and tomorrow they will take yours." The expedition is traditionally regarded as a reconnaissance, though the Secret History of the Mongols and Rashid al-Din name the Cumans, the Alans, Hungary and Rus', Kiev included, as its aims.
sections.forces:
The Rus' army came chiefly from Galicia, Volhynia, Kiev and Chernigov, with some from Smolensk and Turov. Mstislav the Bold, Mstislav III of Kiev and Mstislav of Chernigov were counted the three eldest princes, but the host had no commander-in-chief and each retinue obeyed its own prince. An army sent by Yuri II of Vladimir-Suzdal did not reach the muster. The Cumans were divided into many tribes without a single military organisation; at the Kalka they were commanded by Yarun, the voivode of Mstislav of Galicia.

No primary source gives numbers, and estimates differ widely. Leo de Hartog puts the Rus' army at 30,000 and the Mongols at 20,000; Richard Gabriel and Hector Hugh Munro put the Rus' at 80,000, and Gabriel the Mongols at about 23,000. Russian historians of the Soviet era gave 80,000 to 100,000 for the Rus', but recent ones give far lower figures with the Mongols ahead: D. G. Khrustalev (2013) 10,000 Rus' soldiers including mercenaries and 5,000 Cuman horsemen, Carl Sverdrup 8,000 for the Rus'. Tatishchev gave 103,000 Rus' and 50,000 Cuman horsemen. John Fennell holds that the figures in the Russian sources are formulaic or exaggerated; the Novgorod First Chronicle and the Primary Chronicle imply 11,000 Rus' soldiers, which he also thinks too many. The Armenian historian Sebastatsi gave the Mongols as 20,000 when they first appeared in the Caucasus in 1221.
sections.course:
The princes met at Zarub on the Dnieper. Mongol envoys told them the Mongols had no quarrel with the Rus' and had come against the Cumans; the princes had the envoys killed and the host moved down the Dnieper. Crossing to the left bank, the Rus' met a Mongol advance guard and put it to flight, killing its commander Hamabek. Two weeks later they came to the Kalka and beat a second advance detachment. A council could not decide whether to camp or go forward, and each prince chose his own course.

On the morning of 31 May the allies began to cross the Kalka. The Cuman horse and the Volhynian retinue went first, then the Galicians and the Chernigovians. The Kievan host stayed on the west bank and began to build a fortified camp. The Cumans and Volhynians met the Mongol advance guard and at first did well; Daniel Romanovich of Volhynia was wounded. The advance guard fell back, the Rus' pursued it, lost their order and ran into the main Mongol force. Seeing that the princes behind the Cumans had fallen far back, Subutai ordered his main body to attack, and the Cumans ran.

The Mongol right wing, the wing of attack, succeeded fastest. The fleeing Cumans crushed the Chernigov regiments, which were ready to march, and the Mongols then attacked the Galicians and the Cuman detachments still on their flanks. Mstislav of Lutsk tried to help, then Oleg of Kursk, and both hosts were beaten. Mstislav of Kiev watched from his camp and did not move. Subutai left the khans Tsugir and Teshi to besiege the camp and pursued the survivors with the main body.
sections.aftermath:
Richard Gabriel claims the Rus' lost 50,000 men and the Mongols very few. The Primary Chronicle gives 10,000 killed, the Nikonian Chronicle, written much later, 60,000, and the Novgorod First Chronicle gives no figure but says that only one man in ten came home. At least nine princes died, among them Mstislav of Chernigov, who was lost with his son in the retreat north. The Galician and Volhynian retinues ran to their boats on the Dnieper and cut up the others. Mstislav the Bold reached the west bank and destroyed all the boats he could find.

The Kievan camp had no water. On the third day Ploskinya, a voivode of the brodniks sent by Subutai, swore on the cross that the Kievans would be spared and the princes and commanders freed for ransom. The Mongols, avenging their envoys, broke the promise and attacked as the Kievans came out; some were killed and some taken. The princes and commanders were laid under boards and crushed by the victors, who sat on top to feast. One version holds that the promise had been not to shed blood.

The Mongol scouts reached Novgorod-Svyatopolch. Hearing that Vladimir troops under the 14-year-old Vasilko Konstantinovich of Rostov had arrived at Chernigov, they gave up the march on Kiev and went to the Volga, where the Volga Bulgars beat them at the Battle of Samara Bend; according to Ibn al-Athir only 4,000 survived. They then joined Genghis Khan east of the Syr Darya. Jebe died soon afterwards.
sections.sources:
No Mongol or Cuman account survives. The Rus' chronicles name the princes who took part and who died but say little of the armies or the casualties. The Novgorod First Chronicle, contemporary with the battle and judged the most reliable, blames the flight of the Cumans. The Hypatian Chronicle tells in detail only of the centre, where Daniel, Mstislav of Lutsk and Oleg of Kursk fought, and links the flight to the arrival of fresh Mongol forces, as does the Suzdal Chronicle for the Cumans. Henry of Livonia, writing about 1225, is the only author to give Rus' losses in figures, which he says are very approximate. The Tale of the Battle on the Kalka in the chronicles was probably written soon after.

The tellings of the fighting differ. In another the Mongols retreat for nine days, then halt and form up on the Kalka; Volhynia and Kursk open a gap for the fleeing Cumans, and the Mongol heavy cavalry charge through it; the Chernigov army, not knowing the battle had begun, collides with the Cumans; smoke disrupts the Rus' command; the Mongol wings close round the Rus', though Mstislav the Bold cuts through; and Mstislav of Kiev holds a stockaded camp on a hill by the Dnieper with 10,000 men. In that telling a second Mongol embassy declared war; in the one followed here it was let go in peace. The date is also given differently: by one reckoning the fighting ended on 31 May, three days after the main defeat. The Kalka itself is not identified for certain.
sections.legacy:
The Mongols had not come to conquer and went east after plundering. Many principalities lost much of their armies, with Vladimir-Suzdal the notable exception. The Mongols had crossed most of the Cuman steppe, seen the Rus' forces for themselves and learned from many prisoners how the principalities were organised and fought in different seasons. Subutai left spies in Rus'. More than ten years later the Mongols made their western campaign by the same route in reverse, and in 1237 Subutai and Batu Khan attacked again and conquered the Kievan Rus'.

The retinues of the princes and towns were scattered over a huge territory and weakly linked to one another, and gathering a large force was difficult. The battle appears in the chronicles' Tale of the Battle on the Kalka, in novels by Vasily Yan, Isai Kalashnikov and Aleksei Yugov, in a story by Leonid Leonov, and in a painting by Pavel Ryzhenko. A folklore festival at the Kamennye Mogily reserve commemorates those who died.

summary: At the Kalka River on 31 May 1223 a Mongol army under Jebe and Subutai defeated the Cumans and the Rus' princes of Kiev, Galicia, Volhynia and Chernigov, who had no common commander. The Kievan camp then surrendered and its princes were killed. Numbers are only estimates.
references: John Fennell, The Crisis of Medieval Russia 1200–1304 (Longman, 1983)
Richard Gabriel, Subotai The Valiant: Genghis Khan's Greatest General (Praeger, 2004)
Leo de Hartog, Genghis Khan: Conqueror of the World (I. B. Tauris, 1989)
Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the West, 1221–1410 (Pearson Education, 2005)
Janet Martin, Medieval Russia: 980–1584 (Cambridge University Press, 1995)
notes: Date: the English account dates the battle to 31 May 1223. The Russian introduction says the Cumans and main Rus' forces were beaten first and that 'after 3 days, on 31 May 1223' the fighting ended, but its account of the course has the crossing on the morning of 31 May. I kept 31 May as the date, noted the one-telling variant in facts and sources, and did not date the main defeat.

Mongol strength: de Hartog 20,000 and Gabriel about 23,000 (English); Sebastatsi 20,000 in 1221 (Russian); 20,000 under Jebe and Subutai in 1221-22 (English background). Rus' strength: 30,000 (de Hartog), 80,000 (Gabriel, Munro), 11,000 implied by two chronicles (Fennell doubts it), 10,000 Rus' plus 5,000 Cumans (Khrustalev 2013), 8,000 (Sverdrup), 80,000-100,000 (Soviet era) or 40,000-45,000 (Russian), 103,000 plus 50,000 Cuman horsemen (Tatishchev). Not chosen between.

Losses: Gabriel 50,000 Rus'; Primary Chronicle 10,000; Nikonian 60,000; Novgorod First one in ten came home. The Russian says at least nine princes died. Henry of Livonia's figure appears only as a missing quotation in the Russian text, so I did not give it.

Disagreements between the two accounts: (1) the second Mongol embassy: English has the Mongols send another set declaring war; Russian has the second embassy at Oleshye released in peace. I put the first in sources only. (2) Advance guard: English has a rearguard of 1,000 under Hamabek, killed to the last man, after Mstislav the Bold crossed the Dnieper; Russian has a fight on the left bank, Hamabek killed, and a second advance guard beaten on the Kalka. I followed the Russian. (3) Approach: English has nine days of feigned retreat and a Mongol halt on the Kalka; Russian has two weeks' march. (4) Galicia: English has Galicia and Volhynia sail down the Dnieper and Kiev and Chernigov go up it; Russian has the Galician host go by the Dniester and the Black Sea to the Dnieper's mouth. Left out. (5) The fight: Russian has the Cumans and Volhynians first across, the Kievan camp on the west bank, the Mongol right wing and Lutsk and Kursk coming to help; English has a gap opened by Volhynia and Kursk, smoke, envelopment. Told by the Russian and the other put in sources. (6) Kievan camp: English a hill by the Dnieper with 10,000 men; Russian only the west bank. (7) The princes' death: English says Mstislav of Kiev was executed without shedding blood; Russian says princes and commanders were crushed under boards, with a version of a promise not to shed blood and Vernadsky's explanation (the soul is in the blood), not used. (8) Mstislav of Chernigov: English has him die when his line collapsed; Russian has him lose his life in the retreat with his son (I wrote 'lost with his son in the retreat north' on the Russian wording about the prince).

Left out: Marshall's 'one of the greatest adventures of cavalry warfare', Genghis Khan's praise of his generals, the Venetian alliance, the Soldaia raid, the claim of Jochi's illness, the claim that the battle was 'decisive' (English), the Russian lists of princes, Tolochko's assessment (quotation missing from the saved Russian text), the games and the Medieval: Total War mention.

The 'Kamyani Mohyly' spelling is mine for Каменные могилы, which the Russian names as the reserve; Russian says the festival is held there. The English article's Hamabek is the Russian Ганибек. 'Brodniks' is the Russian term for the people whose voivode Ploskinya was.
The legacy line on feudal fragmentation is the Russian account's general remark on the principalities' military organisation, not a verdict on this battle; cut if too strong.
